difficultyReason: Two-concept conditional gap: stimulus links 'board-certified' to 'authorized to prescribe' and 'prescribing off-label' to 'patient harm risk,' but the conclusion about a specific physician requires the student to supply the connecting conditional. One reversed-conditional trap and one too-weak trap are present.
stimulus: Only physicians who are board-certified in a given specialty are authorized to prescribe medications approved exclusively for that specialty. Dr. Renata Osei holds no board certification in oncology. Therefore, Dr. Osei is not authorized to prescribe any oncology-exclusive medications.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All physicians who are authorized to prescribe oncology-exclusive medications hold board certification in oncology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any physician who holds a board certification in oncology is authorized to prescribe oncology-exclusive medications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most physicians who lack oncology board certification are not authorized to prescribe oncology-exclusive medications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Osei has never attempted to prescribe any oncology-exclusive medication.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No medication can be classified as oncology-exclusive unless it has been reviewed by a board-certified oncologist.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states only board-certified oncologists are authorized to prescribe oncology-exclusive medications. Read carefully: 'only physicians who are board-certified … are authorized' means authorized → board-certified. Since Dr. Osei lacks board certification, she is not authorized. Choice A restates exactly this conditional in the direction needed to run modus tollens: authorized → board-certified; Osei is not board-certified; therefore Osei is not authorized. The conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the contrapositive of the stimulus's 'only' statement made explicit, closing the gap between the general rule and the conclusion about Dr. Osei.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's 'only' clause runs authorized → board-certified; B gives board-certified → authorized, which is the converse and does not force the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too-weak trap. 'Most' does not cover all cases and thus cannot guarantee Dr. Osei — one specific physician — falls under the rule. The conclusion requires certainty, not probability.
explanations.D: Irrelevant to authorization. Whether Dr. Osei has ever attempted to prescribe is a behavioral fact about her past, not about her legal authorization status.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject to the classification of medications, not to physician authorization. Even if true, it does not connect Dr. Osei's lack of certification to her authorization status.

difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in an economics context. Stimulus connects 'price controls' to 'shortages' and 'shortages' to 'black markets,' but the link between price controls and the specific conclusion about black markets requires students to supply the missing premise. Partial-bridge and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: Economists have long observed that whenever a government imposes price controls that hold prices below market equilibrium, shortages inevitably follow. The legislature of Valdoria has just enacted a law capping the price of residential heating fuel well below its current market price. Clearly, a black market for heating fuel will emerge in Valdoria.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortages of essential commodities, such as heating fuel, always give rise to black markets for those commodities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Valdoria's legislature was aware that price controls tend to produce shortages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Black markets are more likely to develop when consumers strongly depend on the controlled commodity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some governments that impose price controls eventually repeal them when black markets appear.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Price controls below market equilibrium sometimes lead to black markets in the affected sector.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: (1) price controls below equilibrium → shortages; (2) Valdoria has enacted such controls; therefore a black market will emerge. The missing link is shortages → black markets. Choice A supplies exactly this universal conditional, closing the chain and making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Correct. It provides the universal conditional (shortages → black markets) that completes the two-step chain: price controls → shortages → black markets. Together with the premise about Valdoria's law, the conclusion follows by necessity.
explanations.B: The legislature's awareness is irrelevant to whether a shortage or black market will in fact occur. Knowing about an effect does not prevent or cause it.
explanations.C: Too-weak trap. 'More likely' raises probability but does not guarantee a black market will emerge, which is what the conclusion asserts.
explanations.D: This describes a possible governmental response after black markets appear, not a premise that forces black markets to appear in the first place.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Sometimes' does not force the conclusion that a black market will certainly emerge in Valdoria's specific case.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an environmental-science context. Stimulus requires students to connect 'releases above threshold levels' to 'legally liable,' using a conditional involving a specific actor. Reversed-conditional and partial-bridge traps are present.
stimulus: Under the Clearwater Environmental Compact, any industrial facility that releases pollutants above established threshold levels into the river basin is legally liable for remediation costs. Investigators have confirmed that the Harwick Processing Plant released effluents containing mercury at concentrations three times above the established threshold. The Harwick Processing Plant is therefore legally liable for remediation costs.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercury is among the pollutants covered by the established thresholds under the Clearwater Environmental Compact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industrial facilities that are legally liable for remediation costs are always those that release mercury specifically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Harwick Processing Plant is the primary source of mercury contamination in the river basin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any facility found liable under the Clearwater Environmental Compact will be required to cease operations until remediation is complete.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory investigators are authorized to determine which facilities have exceeded threshold levels under the Clearwater Environmental Compact.

explanations.correct: The Compact imposes liability for releasing 'pollutants above established threshold levels.' The stimulus establishes that Harwick released mercury above threshold concentrations. The gap: is mercury a pollutant covered by those thresholds? Choice A closes this gap explicitly, ensuring that Harwick's mercury release falls within the Compact's scope, making the liability conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Correct. Without confirming that mercury is a covered pollutant under the Compact's thresholds, the general rule cannot be applied to Harwick's mercury releases. A supplies this missing link, completing the syllogism.
explanations.B: Reversed-scope trap. The Compact's rule is: above threshold → liable. B inverts the relationship by implying liability requires mercury specifically, which is both too narrow and runs the conditional backward.
explanations.C: Harwick being the primary source establishes degree of contribution, not legal liability under the Compact's threshold rule. Primary source status is irrelevant to whether the threshold criterion is met.
explanations.D: This describes a consequence of liability (cease operations), not a condition for establishing it. It does not help connect Harwick's conduct to liability.
explanations.E: Investigator authorization concerns procedural legitimacy of the finding, not whether the substantive legal standard for liability is satisfied.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap bridging linguistic classification to policy entitlement in a policy/linguistics context. Correct answer requires a universal conditional linking a category ('recognized minority language') to an entitlement ('public instruction funding'). Too-weak and subject-shift traps are present.
stimulus: The Regional Language Board classifies Sorranic as a recognized minority language of the province. Under provincial law, communities whose primary language is a recognized minority language are entitled to receive public funding for instruction in that language. The Sorranic-speaking community of Aldenmere has therefore been incorrectly denied public funding for Sorranic-language instruction.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldenmere is a community whose primary language is Sorranic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most communities in the province whose primary language is a recognized minority language have received public funding for instruction in that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Regional Language Board has the authority to compel the provincial government to fund minority-language instruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aldenmere has applied for public funding for Sorranic-language instruction on at least one prior occasion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any community denied funding to which it is legally entitled has been incorrectly denied that funding.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain runs: (1) Sorranic is a recognized minority language; (2) communities whose primary language is a recognized minority language are entitled to funding; (3) therefore Aldenmere has been incorrectly denied funding. The gap: Is Aldenmere a community whose primary language is Sorranic? The stimulus calls Aldenmere 'the Sorranic-speaking community' but does not explicitly state it is a community 'whose primary language is Sorranic' — the legal trigger. Choice A supplies exactly this missing predicate, closing the syllogism and making the conclusion necessary. (Note: the conclusion also implicitly requires that denial of an entitlement is 'incorrect,' but that normative link is built into the word 'entitled' in the premise; the factual gap closed by A is the operative missing link.)
explanations.A: Correct. Once Aldenmere is confirmed as a community whose primary language is Sorranic, it falls squarely under the provincial law's entitlement provision, and denying it funding is logically incorrect.
explanations.B: Too-weak trap. 'Most communities' receiving funding does not guarantee Aldenmere is entitled and has been incorrectly denied; 'most' leaves open that Aldenmere could be an exception.
explanations.C: Subject-shift trap. The Board's compellability authority is irrelevant to whether Aldenmere is legally entitled and has been incorrectly denied. The conclusion is about entitlement, not enforcement power.
explanations.D: Whether Aldenmere applied previously does not establish legal entitlement or that the denial was incorrect. Prior application is irrelevant to the substantive legal question.
explanations.E: This is a tautological restatement of what 'incorrectly denied' already implies and does not supply the missing factual link — that Aldenmere is entitled in the first place. Without A, E alone cannot force the conclusion.
